ranking.note: Raised to P1: fixes an actual hang reproducible from any binding whose GC finalizer logs during a kernel log callback; reliability defect at the API boundary outranks the feature work it was scored below.
Raised to P1: same deadlock/thread-serialization defect as #36768; the two are competing fixes and a decision is what is blocking the fix from landing.
Raised to P1: fixes an unintended per-call copy of caller txdata in the kernel verification C API (orders-of-magnitude cost to every external consumer) plus removes a stale-sighash-state hazard.
Moved up 11: it is the logging-macro prerequisite for #33847/#30342 and cannot sit below the PRs it unblocks.
Moved up 8: it is the base of the pruning chain (#36854, #36856, #36857) and must be reviewed before them.

Moved down 10: broad pure refactor of fatal-error plumbing whose value overlaps #35646 and #36326, and it sits behind base PR #25665; less immediate consumer benefit than the API-completeness work above it.
Moved down 7: decoupling from translation is durable boundary work but no consumer is blocked on it today, unlike the logging and pruning chains above.
Lowered to P3: compile-time-disabled, narrow tooling feature with a single prototype consumer; deferrable next to the API-completeness and boundary-correctness P2s.

inconsistencies: #34775 and #36768 fix the same defect (log callbacks invoked under the logger mutex, deadlocking re-entrant/GC callbacks) by incompatible means; review #36768 first as the explicitly-framed alternative, then close or rebase the other — do not review them independently.

Design conflict: #34775 restricts libbitcoinkernel to a single process-wide logging connection, while #33847/#30342 move toward per-context connections with per-connection levels. The same reviewer pass should settle the direction, otherwise one line of work invalidates the other's API.
Logging chain order matters: #34778 (outside this list) -> #29256 -> #33847 -> #30342 -> #30343. #29256 was scored well below the PRs it unblocks; it must be reviewed first.
Pruning chain order matters: #36739 -> #36854 -> #36856 -> #36857, with #36738 (outside this list) also a base for #36856 and #36858. #36739 was scored below its dependents.

#36909 and #36911 add alternative APIs for the same O(n^2) witness-stack read problem; they are mutually redundant and should be decided together rather than both merged. #36911 explicitly positions itself as the alternative to #36909.

Three PRs restructure fatal/flush error propagation at the kernel boundary: #29700 (util::Result/FlushResult returns), #35646 (drop M_ERROR, util::Expected<T, FatalError>), #36326 (typed FatalError/FlushError notifications), with #34132 additionally changing when dbwrapper aborts. Their designs overlap and will conflict; agree on one error model before merging any of them. #35646 is a stated prerequisite for #35570.
#32427 removes the LevelDB BlockTreeDB entirely while #34132 changes LevelDB read-failure semantics in CDBWrapper; coordinate so the latter is not written against storage that the former deletes.

Kernel/validation straddle: #32427, #35187, #34132 and #35662 change validation or storage behaviour as well as the kernel API and may need splitting along that line; #35570 and #36318 are validation-signature changes justified mainly by kernel API cleanliness.
result.notes: The category is dominated by one project's boundary work, so the original assessment put almost everything in P2. I kept P2 broad but pulled out a P1 tier for the concrete reliability/performance defects consumers hit today (the log-callback deadlock pair and the sighash copy), and left the deferrable interface polish, duplicate witness-stack APIs and the doc warning in P3. Two large feature PRs (#32427, #35187) sit at the top of P2 rather than P1 because they add capability rather than resolve something harmful; draft/paused status played no part in that.
